p01.why: The heads are equivalent without constraints and the parameter lists match, so the more constrained Strong template wins and returns One.

p02.why: With auto there is no target type; both f satisfy their constraints for char, and the lists differ in length, so constraints do not remove either one and two functions remain.

p03.why: Only the first parameter takes part and they tie; the defaulted parameter counts at the pack's position (Q-0216), so ORD-12 does not apply and the call is ambiguous. GCC and EDG choose the template with no pack.

p04.why: The swapped candidate's parameters are reversed, after which the T* const& template is more specialized and returns true. GCC does not reverse and fails the static_assert (Q-0211).

p05.why: auto** is more specialized than auto*, which is more specialized than the primary, so the three values are 0, 1, and 2.

p06.why: The member's object parameter Item& makes the parameter lists the same, so the constrained template wins in both cases. Clang 18 finds both calls ambiguous.

p07.why: Only the result types take part and they are the same T*, so the constrained conversion wins for int and p points to b.

p08.why: The two partial specializations have the same pattern and equivalent heads, so the constrained one wins for int* and only the plain one matches char*.

p09.why: The int V partial specialization is more specialized than the auto V primary.

p10.why: List<T, A&...> is more specialized than List<T, A...>, and List<int, float> matches only the first template.

p11.why: Both object parameters are lvalue references to Box, and T* is more specialized than T, so take returns Ptr.

p12.why: The explicit specialization and explicit instantiation pick which(T*); the int* call selects which(T*) whose int* specialization returns 3, and char* gives 2.

p13.why: For an lvalue argument the lvalue reference template is more specialized, so f(n) returns One.

p14.why: T* is more specialized than T, and const T* more than T*, as in the page example.

p15.why: The member's object parameter Item& matches the free function's first parameter, so the two tie and the call is ambiguous.

p16.why: Only the first parameter takes part, the templates tie, and no tie-breaker applies, so f(1) is ambiguous.

p17.why: const and volatile are not a superset of each other, so neither pair direction is removed and the call is ambiguous.

p18.why: Each initialization chooses the template the page table names (T&, const T&, const T&, const T&&), so no static_assert in an unchosen body is instantiated.

p19.why: pair(T, T) is more specialized than pair(T, U) for (1, 2), and only pair(T, U) is viable for (1, 'c').

p20.why: R appears in no compared type and needs no value, so f(T*) is more specialized and returns Two.

p21.why: T and T&& both deduce from each other after stripping, and ORD-10 needs two references, so the call is ambiguous.

p22.why: ORD-10 removes one direction and ORD-11 the other, so neither conversion is more specialized. Q-0217: GCC and EDG choose T&.

p23.why: The member's object parameter (X& and Y&&) matches the free template's first parameter, and T* is more specialized than U, so both give One.

p24.why: Both candidates are swapped and reversed alike, and the V<T*>, W<T*> template is more specialized, so w == v is true.

p25.why: const T& is more qualified than T&, so f(c) returns Two.

p26.why: The whole function types take part, so T* make(int) is more specialized than T make(int), and f(T*) more than f(T).

p27.why: The member with no ref-qualifier gets an rvalue reference object parameter against X&&, so the two tie and the call is ambiguous. Clang 18 and EDG choose the member (Q-0214).

p28.why: The page Evidence records that every compiler but GCC 14 chooses read(T&) for this address; the rules do not show me how ORD-9 orders T& against T&&.

p29.why: The first pair prefers the T& template by ORD-10 and the second pair prefers U*, so the pairs disagree and the call is ambiguous.

p30.why: The result types T* and T* const become the same after stripping, no tie-breaker applies, and the initialization is ambiguous.

p31.why: Each call picks the most specialized viable template: One for List<>, Two for List<int, float>, and Three for the other two.

p32.why: Both object parameters are rvalue references, and T* is more specialized than T, so take returns Ptr.

p33.why: U appears only in a non-deduced position, so each direction fails and the call is ambiguous.

p34.why: The placement delete template with T* is more specialized and is called when the constructor throws; the other template is never instantiated.

p35.why: Only the result types take part, and T* is more specialized than T, so p points to second.

p36.why: The templates tie in ordering, and their heads differ, so the constraint does not decide and the call is ambiguous. EDG may accept (Q-0146).

p37.why: The swapped member gets its object parameter before the reversal, which makes it more specialized, so p == x is true. GCC and EDG choose the non-member (Q-0218).

p38.why: Each pair prefers a different template by ORD-10, so the call is ambiguous.

p39.why: Id<A>::type stays unresolved in one direction, so f(T*, T*) is more specialized and returns Two.

p40.why: The results tie in ordering, but T* and T* const are not the same result type, so the constraint does not decide and the initialization is ambiguous. EDG may accept (Q-0146).

p41.why: The ellipsis takes no part and the constraint decides for the constrained template (Q-0293). GCC finds the call ambiguous.

p42.why: The const member gets the object parameter const Grid&, and T* is more specialized than T, so the result is Ptr. EDG finds the call ambiguous (Q-0398).

p43.why: An invented pack gives no value to T, so the templates without a leading pack win; g(T, Ts...) is more specialized than g(Ts...) for each call.

p44.why: Each specialization selects the most specialized matching partial specialization, as in the page example; T* const* is more specialized than T*.

p45.why: The defaulted parameter and the ellipsis take no part, so T* against T decides for One in both calls.

p46.why: ORD-10 makes T& more specialized than T&& before the pack tie-breaker, so the call returns One.

p47.why: The function types form one pair, so read(T&) is more specialized. Clang finds the address ambiguous (Q-0396).

p48.why: The T* placement delete is more specialized and sets called to 1, so main returns 0.

p49.why: The two partial specializations have different patterns, so the constraint does not decide and Pair<int, int> is ambiguous.

p50.why: The invented type parameter makes the heads equivalent, so the Strong template is more constrained and returns One.

p51.why: T and const T& tie, and ORD-11 needs two references, so the call is ambiguous.

p52.why: The lists differ in length when the defaulted parameter counts, so the constraint does not decide and the call is ambiguous.

p53.why: Both members are swapped candidates, and the W<T*> member is more specialized, so w == x is true.

p54.why: U appears in no compared type, so f(T*) is more specialized and returns Two.

p55.why: Each template fails one pair in the other direction, so neither is more specialized.

p56.why: The int V partial specialization is more specialized than the constrained auto V one because their heads differ. EDG chooses the constrained one (Q-0397).

p57.why: For f(1) the empty pack takes no part and ORD-12 prefers f(T); f(1, 2) matches only the pack template.

p58.why: Id<A>::type matches neither A nor int, so f(T, T) and g(T, int) are more specialized and both give Two.
